name: Self-ligating braces (Damon)
lead: Self-ligating braces are fixed orthodontic brackets that hold the archwire with a built-in clip or slide rather than with elastic or wire ties. They are described as the second most common type of braces, and the Damon system is one commercial brand of them [1].

Braces straighten crowded, gapped or misaligned teeth, which changes the look of the smile and, for some bite problems, the lower face. People choose self-ligating brackets because manufacturers and some clinicians have said the design lowers friction, shortens treatment, reduces discomfort and requires fewer appointments [1]. Systematic reviews of randomized trials have compared conventional, passive self-ligating and active self-ligating brackets on treatment efficiency [2].
Evidence available is limited to a network meta-analysis, comparative and retrospective clinical studies, and laboratory or microbiological work [2][3][4][5].

About six months to two and a half years for braces generally; adjustments every three to six weeks [1]

paras: Instead of securing the archwire with elastic bands or steel ties, self-ligating brackets use a door, clip or slide integrated into the bracket.[1] Studies distinguish passive designs, where the clip does not press on the wire, from active designs, where it does.[2]

Wikipedia's braces article lists other options alongside them: traditional stainless-steel brackets, gold-plated and titanium brackets (often chosen for nickel allergy or looks), lingual braces bonded behind the teeth, and removable clear aligners, which it says are generally not used for complex extraction, surgical or palate-expansion cases [1].

Popular descriptions of self-ligating braces state that treatment time is reduced and that there is less pain and fewer adjustments than with conventional braces; these statements are not attributed to specific studies in the encyclopedic source.[1]

A 2021 systematic review and network meta-analysis restricted to randomized and split-mouth trials tested whether treatment efficiency differs between conventional, passive self-ligating and active self-ligating brackets [2].

The review searched three databases to January 2019 and included 30 randomized trials and 9 split-mouth studies, analysing outcomes such as treatment duration, number of visits, alignment rate, space closure, anchorage loss, bond failure, root resorption, discomfort and quality of life [2]. Of 85 comparisons, only 16 showed statistically significant differences; one reported difference was that archwires were quicker to untie and ligate with active self-ligating ceramic brackets than with conventional ceramic ones [2].

A retrospective study followed 30 adolescents treated with self-ligating brackets for a mean of about 7 years after treatment and compared long-term stability with 30 treated with conventional brackets [3]. A study of 46 adults with narrowed, deformed dental arches compared passive self-ligating braces with early elastics and broad archwires against ligature braces, and reported larger arch widths in the self-ligating group [8].

Fixed braces in general are associated with plaque accumulation and mild gingivitis, with possible gum recession if cleaning is poor, some degree of root resorption in most movement, and pain that rises with force applied.[1] White spot lesions around brackets are a documented complication of orthodontic treatment.[6]

Laboratory studies have compared microbial adhesion on metal, ceramic and self-ligating brackets and on different wire types, and a prospective cohort of 15 patients examined changes in oral bacteria and salivary markers during fixed-appliance treatment.[4][5]

A review of white spot lesions during orthodontic treatment reported that incidence varied widely with technique and was highest with conventional braces, followed by self-ligating braces, and lowest with aligners [6]. In a prospective cohort of 15 fixed-appliance patients, S. mutans levels in saliva rose at 18 months and were higher with conventional braces than with self-ligating braces [5]. Wikipedia notes that most tooth movement causes some root resorption, usually not clinically significant, and that soreness after fitting increases with force applied [1].

Randomized and split-mouth trials of self-ligating versus conventional brackets were pooled in a 2021 network meta-analysis of treatment efficiency.[2] A long-term retrospective comparison of 60 adolescents examined stability.[3] A small prospective cohort of 15 patients examined saliva and microbiology during fixed-appliance treatment generally.[5]

Orthodontic appearance goals are often the draw: Wikipedia notes that cosmetic use of braces is more common in wealthier countries, and in North America most treatment is delivered by orthodontists [1]. The Damon name is a commercial system rather than a separate technique, and Wikipedia's braces article does not describe its history or inventor [1].

card.summary: Braces whose brackets clip the wire themselves, marketed as faster and gentler; trial reviews have compared them against conventional brackets.
card.aka: Damon braces, self-ligating brackets, passive/active SL brackets
card.note: Manufacturer claims of speed and comfort are not clearly attributed to trial evidence in encyclopedic sources.

quick.overview:
Self-ligating braces are metal or ceramic brackets with a built-in clip that holds the wire, so no elastic ties are needed. Damon is the best-known system.

Proponents describe shorter treatment, less pain and fewer visits. A network meta-analysis of randomized trials has examined whether efficiency differs from conventional brackets.
quick.mechanism: The built-in clip is meant to let the archwire slide with less restriction. Teeth move in response to the wire's force, as with any fixed braces.
quick.risks: Risks resemble those of fixed braces generally: plaque build-up and gum inflammation, white spot lesions, some root resorption and discomfort.

angle.text: Like any fixed braces, self-ligating brackets move teeth into better alignment, which is the appearance benefit. The self-ligating feature is the delivery mechanism and is promoted for comfort, fewer visits and lower friction.
